flashcards.q: What does CI validate for a model that classic software CI does not?
flashcards.a: Data validation (schema, nulls, drift) before training, model validation (eval against a fixed held-out set compared to the current champion's metric, not just an absolute threshold), and input/output contract validation.

flashcards.q: Why does shadow deployment need less traffic than an unpaired canary to detect a real difference?
flashcards.a: Shadow sends the SAME request to both models -- paired observations -- so shared request-level noise cancels out in the paired difference, unlike an unpaired comparison across two separate traffic groups.

flashcards.q: What can shadow deployment never prove, no matter how much traffic it processes?
flashcards.a: Whether a prediction difference actually improves a real business outcome -- the shadow model's output is logged but never served or acted on, so the causal path from prediction to outcome is never tested.

flashcards.q: What's the real cost of running shadow deployment?
flashcards.a: Doubled inference infrastructure for the whole shadow window (both models process 100% of traffic), added request-mirroring complexity, and risk that the shadow harness doesn't fully replicate production timing/feature computation.

flashcards.q: What's the most common gap between textbook canary process and what teams actually do?
flashcards.a: Ramping traffic percentage (1% -> 20% -> 50%) based on a dashboard glance and gut feel rather than a pre-registered minimum sample size and significance threshold defined before the canary started.

flashcards.q: Name the four components a complete model rollback needs to cover.
flashcards.a: 1) serving container, 2) response/feature cache (version-tag or invalidate), 3) feature pipeline (confirm it still matches the schema the prior version expects), 4) batch/offline scoring jobs (separate schedule, won't auto-follow a serving-only rollback).

flashcards.q: How can a rollback itself introduce training-serving skew?
flashcards.a: If the feature pipeline moved forward to support the newer model version and isn't also reverted or version-gated, the rolled-back-to older model now receives features in a shape/distribution it was never trained on -- a mismatch the rollback itself created.

flashcards.q: What is 'version drift' in a production ML system?
flashcards.a: Different requests served by an inconsistent mix of model versions across serving, cache, and batch jobs -- invisible until predictions diverge, and only detectable with per-request version logging (not just checking a deploy dashboard).

flashcards.q: Why can't shadow deployment validate a contextual bandit's real behavior?
flashcards.a: A bandit's future decisions depend on its own past served actions (exploration/exploitation history) -- shadow logs what it WOULD have shown, but never generates the real served-action history that drives the bandit's actual future inputs.

flashcards.q: When would you choose roll-forward over rollback?
flashcards.a: When root cause is well understood and a targeted fix is faster/safer than reverting -- especially if downstream state (cache, features) has already diverged enough that reverting would itself reintroduce version-drift problems. Unknown root cause + active user impact -> rollback first.

flashcards.q: For a fraud-detection model canary, which metric do teams most often forget to gate rollback on?
flashcards.a: False-positive rate, not just fraud-catch-rate (recall) -- a model that catches more fraud but blocks significantly more legitimate transactions looks like an improvement on the primary metric while regressing user experience and revenue.

flashcards.q: Why should prompt/fine-tune changes go through the same shadow/canary/rollback discipline as model retrains?
flashcards.a: A prompt wording change or fine-tune can have the same blast radius as a full model swap on output quality and safety, but is often treated as a low-stakes text edit shipped with no eval gate -- exactly the gap that causes prompt regressions to reach production.
